items.title: He Was Hugely Influential. He Also Had a Foolish Streak.
items.summary: I n his memoirs, Giacomo Casanova, the 18th-century writer and libertine, made a helpful distinction between “stupid” people and “fools.” Those who are stupid, he opined, were generally honest and merely lacking in education: “They are like eyes that, if not for their cataracts, would be very beautiful.” Fools, however, he couldn’t abide. He found them conceited and insolent. Worst of all, he wrote, “I feel like a fool whenever I find myself in their company.” We are all, I take Casanova to be saying, stupid to some degree. But it takes a special kind of obliviousness to be a fool. The novelist and art critic John Berger was neither insolent nor conceited, and he was less stupid than most of us. But he undoubtedly had a foolish streak. Berger would have turned 100 this year. He is the subject of a new biography, John Berger: From Life , by Tom Overton, an archive curator at the Barbican Centre, in London, and nearly a decade after his death, at age 90, many of his books are being reissued. Berger was an experimentalist. Apart from his art criticism and fiction, he wrote screenplays, painted, and drew. But he is best known for Ways of Seeing , a 1972 TV series about art and power that is still a staple of art education more than 50 years after it was first aired on the BBC. To rewatch Ways of Seeing , which consists of four 30-minute episodes, is to realize how immensely influential it has been. Like a brilliant college lecturer, Berger methodically builds arguments around four themes: the effects of reproduction on original artworks; art’s role in the objectification of women; the part art has played in establishing social status and ownership; and the reality-distorting role of modern advertising. Berger gets his points across with almost electrifying immediacy. When he presents directly to the camera, you can feel his magnetism instantly. His flaring eyes, mobile brow, and slight difficulty pronouncing the r sound convey his intelligence and moral seriousness with almost comical exaggeration. But Berger’s particular species of charisma was inseparable from his earnestness, which had a relentless quality. Behind it lurked a sort of wet-eyed, slightly indiscriminate craving for human connection. Berger created Ways of Seeing with the producer and director Mike Dibb. A subsequent book , adapted from the series, was a collaboration credited to Berger and four others. The series was interpreted by some as a rebuke to Civilisation , a 13-part documentary from 1969 about European visual culture that was commissioned for the BBC by David Attenborough and presented by Kenneth Clark. But Berger’s early career owed a great deal to Clark, an acclaimed art historian who had been the director of London’s National Gallery, and his shorter TV series was a different project with a narrower aim. [ Read: The seminal TV series that changed how we see ] The title was very much to the point. As if in emulation of his father, who tended to soldiers with damaged eyesight during World War I, he saw himself as removing cataracts from people’s eyes. Berger wrote from a position of principled belief and always from the heart. He was a Marxist who wanted to rescue people from their naivete about the workings of capitalism. In the introduction to Permanent Red , his first collection of essays, he was forthright about his criteria for judging art: “The question I ask is: Does this work help or encourage men to know and claim their social rights?” It’s this quality of yearning—for love, for justice, for compassion—that is still the main reason to read Berger. In his essays and reviews, something deeper than aesthetic judgment always feels at stake. But when you compare his art writing with that of his sharper, less sentimental contemporaries—Susan Sontag, Robert Hughes, Peter Schjeldahl, Janet Malcolm—you’re reminded of Berger’s tendency to belabor the obvious. A plodding, pedagogical flavor compromises much of his criticism (“to return now to our original question”), as if he worried that too much humor or writerly flair might nibble away at his class credentials. Berger understood that images play a huge role in projecting the influence of capital and making wealth enviable. Ways of Seeing demonstrated this in its four pithy episodes. It was an effort to awaken the public to the ways in which injustice was embedded in both the art in our museums and the imagery disseminated across Western culture. Berger derived his insights not only from Karl Marx but also from Marxist thinkers in the 20th century, including his friend Frederick Antal, the pioneering Hungarian art historian who wrote about the social background of Florentine art during the Renaissance; Georg Lukács, the Leninist literary critic and philosopher; and Walter Benjamin, the great media theorist and cultural critic. But Berger’s 1970s-style “consciousness-raising” was aimed at a broad public and proved very successful. Even now, when his critiques have become platitudes, to hear him speak about the male gaze or the depredations of advertising is to feel these notions reinfused with amplitude and urgency. Ways of Seeing catapulted the show’s presenter to fame. That fame turned to notoriety later in 1972, when Berger’s experimental novel G. —about a Casanova-like character caught up in political events around the turn of the 20th century—won the Booker Prize. The book, which Berger spent five years writing, is dedicated to his partner Anya Bostock, an acclaimed translator, and to “her sisters in Women’s Liberation.” This was painful—for Bostock, anyway—because while writing it, Berger had begun an affair with another woman, Annar Cassam. Bostock believed that G. , with its libertine hero, was partly Berger’s attempt to use fiction to understand his own behavior. ( G. might be better recalled today for Berger’s Booker Prize–acceptance speech, in which he criticized the company behind the prize for historically profiting from enslaved labor in the Caribbean; his protest was an attempt, he said, to “turn this prize against itself.”) Overton’s biography provides a useful critical overview of Berger’s writing, as well as of his work for television and radio. Its author, who became close friends with Berger when he cataloged the latter’s archive for the British Library, refers to his subject throughout as “John.” But intermittently, Overton switches to “you,” addressing Berger as if he were still alive and might be able to account for himself. The habit kicks in when Overton is most dismayed by what he has learned about Berger’s unfeeling treatment of his various lovers or of his son Jacob, who made a film that drew on Berger’s life—just as Berger had often used others’ lives in his writing—resulting in a rift that lasted years. Overton’s use of direct address appears to be his way of enacting the special difficulty he faces as Berger’s biographer, effectively letting us listen in as he asks, What do I owe to my subject, who was my friend but is now dead? The question of what we owe the dead obsessed Berger. His preoccupation had its roots in his father’s experiences during World War I. In the wake of that catastrophe, the British fixated on memorializing the dead. Monuments were erected in nearly every village square. Born in 1926, Berger came to believe that humans live along two axes: the horizontal line, which relates to one’s physical place in the world, and the vertical line of time, which connects the living with the dead and those yet to be born. His understanding of the importance of place fed into his writing about migrants displaced by war and the movements of capital. But for Berger, that relationship between the living and the dead was, “almost as soon as he began to think about it, the very core of politics.” “The one question of his work,” Overton believes, “was: how do we live with the dead?” James Fitton, Ruskin Spear, John Berger and John Minton in 1950 (Frank Lilley / Hulton Archive / Getty) The questio

items.title: Why smart people stay stuck in research mode
items.summary: I recently had coffee with a university colleague who told me she was in the middle of planning a workshop. She had bought a couple of books about hosting workshops, had created a spreadsheet projecting attendance under different scenarios, and was now comparing ticketing platforms. But she still hadn’t invited a single person. We talked about how none of that research was necessarily a waste of time. When you love learning, figuring out the best approach can be enjoyable in itself. But every answer can produce another question, and before you know it, preparation has become the project. Worse, that endless research keeps you busy while the harder questions wait: Will anybody be interested? Am I any good at this? The psychology of endless research You could call this a problem of overthinking, but research points instead to several nuanced and overlapping tendencies that can make gathering information feel easier, safer, and more satisfying than taking action. A better option could be hiding somewhere. You might find a venue that suits your workshop and still spend another weekend looking because there might be an even better option out there. Psychologists call this tendency to seek the best possible choice maximizing , and studies suggest that people higher in maximizing tendency explore more alternatives before selecting one. Research feels like a respectable form of avoidance. The task we’re avoiding may expose us to rejection, uncertainty, or embarrassment; reading about it does not. In that way, psychologists have argued that procrastination can serve as a form of short-term mood regulation, which is why we often find ourselves opening another tab instead of taking action. Thinking itself can feel rewarding. Psychologists use the term need for cognition to describe how much people enjoy sustained mental effort. People higher in this trait tend to put more effort into decisions and are less inclined to change their research approach under time pressure. Without a clear sense of when to stop, it’s easy to keep looking. Researchers found that participants with a stronger need for certainty spend longer gathering information, particularly when there is no clear rule for making a choice. You might have studied many different ways to run workshops, without knowing what would make one preferable to the others. Reading more about each approach may give you a better understanding of your options without bringing you any closer to a decision. Taken together, these tendencies help explain why the research phase of a project can be so tempting to linger in. Depending on your intellectual curiosity and how you respond to uncertainty, mapping possibilities and comparing approaches can feel more rewarding than the practical work of bringing an idea to life. This isn’t limited to professional projects — the same pattern can show up when you’re exploring a new hobby or trying to change a habit. You can spend weeks learning about something without ever taking action to find out what it’s like to actually do it. How to turn research into action If you tend to get stuck in research mode, you don’t need to force yourself to become less curious. You just need to recognize when you’ve learned enough theory, and when your question can only be answered through direct experience. Here are three simple steps you can follow to put what you’ve learned into practice and use the results to decide what to do next: 1. First, take stock of what you know. Write down what you’ve already learned about the different moving parts of the project. Alongside it, list the concrete ideas you could act on. You’ll probably find that your bottleneck isn’t more theoretical knowledge, but evidence and direct experience from the real world. 2. Next, run a tiny experiment. Decide what you will test and the trial period, using this mini protocol: I will [action] for [duration]. For the would-be workshop organizer, this could be: “I will invite three people to a 30-minute pilot session each week for three weeks.” The point isn’t to figure out every single detail, but to collect the real-world data no comparison chart can ever tell you: whether people show up, the questions they ask, and what parts you enjoy running. 3. Finally, reflect before deciding on your next steps. What surprised you? What would you change? Use those observations to design another tiny experiment or — if you do need to conduct more research — to explore a more focused question with a clear stopping rule for making a choice. Good research helps us make better decisions, but there are questions it simply cannot answer without real-world data. By applying an experimental mindset , you can gather evidence about what works, what doesn’t, and what you still need to figure out. You may still have plenty of questions after your first experiment. Some might send you back to your research, this time with a clearer idea of what you’re looking for. Others may turn out to be far less important than you imagined. The only way to find out is to try something and see what actually happens. And in the meantime, you’ll have made some progress on bringing your idea to life. This article Why smart people stay stuck in research mode is featured on Big Think .

items.title: An Adaptation That’s Both ‘Excellent’ and ‘Bizarre’
items.summary: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. Somewhere in the back of my closet sits a strange relic: a virtual-reality viewer made of cardboard. The only thing I remember watching on it, in 2017, was a 10-minute adaptation of George Saunders’s Booker Prize–winning debut novel, Lincoln in the Bardo . Produced by The New York Times , this 3-D, 360-degree experience was effectively a staged excerpt of the book—which features Abraham Lincoln, his freshly dead 11-year-old son, and a chorus of grotesque ghosts—that could be viewed in full only by constantly swiveling one’s head. Google Cardboard, as this tech was known, was discontinued long ago; a decade later, the most notable thing about this experiment is that it was not the first or the last unconventional incarnation of Saunders’s highly unconventional novel. This week, the Atlantic senior editor Talya Zax admired the boldness of the book’s latest adaptation , an “excellent” and “bizarre” staging at New York’s Metropolitan Opera. Her essay inspired me to dip into the Bardo audiobook, which is memorable for being packed with 166 narrators, many of them celebrities . Spoiler: It holds up. First, here are six new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: The rise of the sexy-cozy autumn read Celebrity has become a jobs program. The Greek island that taught me the art of living “Peeling the Orange,” a poem by Howard Altmann Democrats are sounding more like Republicans. How the American Girl doll lost its way Zax argues that Bardo benefits from opera’s “freedom to be outlandish,” and that a film version would have to contend instead with Hollywood’s “risk-averse studio system.” The book is surreal, full of overlapping dialogue, madcap characters, and descriptions that defy any visual logic. This much is immediately clear, however: Willie Lincoln, the president’s deceased son, is in a sort of graveyard purgatory, which he must escape before it destroys him. Helping him are three oddly contorted ghosts—a mysteriously damned reverend, a priapic printmaker who never consummated his marriage, and a gay man who died by suicide. Telling the story of Lincoln’s grief at the height of the Civil War, Saunders alternates between snippets from the historical record and the cemetery’s giant cast of specters. This is certainly the stuff of opera. It is also fodder for an audiobook that rises above its stunt casting. The recording’s collection of notables resembles the slate of an animated Disney movie motivated by star power: Susan Sarandon, Julianne Moore, Ben Stiller, Don Cheadle, Bill Hader, Lena Dunham, Carrie Brownstein, and Keegan-Michael Key all voice characters. The A-listers get the plum roles, of course, and many of them do effectively dramatize the material; Dunham’s teenage girl is affectingly tormented, Key’s enslaved shade righteously wrathful, Hader’s low-class brawler fabulously profane. The documentary snippets are less effective, voiced largely by colleagues and friends, including 60 employees of Saunders’s publisher, Penguin Random House. Then again, this may have as much to do with the doldrums in those segments of the book as the talent of the cast. The standout performances, however, are from Nick Offerman, David Sedaris, and Saunders himself as Willie’s three helpful ghosts. They have the best material, including sections in which they inhabit the (technically nonspeaking) president’s thoughts. And they showcase what’s best about any effective audiobook. It’s a dramatic rendering, to a degree, but it preserves the interiority and verbal dexterity that only a novel can hold. The banter among this trio is crisp, funny, and layered with meaning, and the soliloquies reminded me that this is Saunders at the height of his power, balancing satire and pathos better than almost any writer I can think of. This eccentric recording is mainstream in one important way: It delivers on its promise of rendering the book faithfully and with a generous dose of flair. What to Read Beloved , by Toni Morrison Beloved asks readers to imagine something as pure and perfect as love—a mother caring for her child; two broken people trying to make something beautiful—in the face of absolute misery and ugliness. That’s where the book’s potency comes from: the tension between the darkness and the light. Sethe, its main character, has committed unspeakable violence toward her own daughter, but she was motivated by maternal devotion. Having survived that transformational tragedy, she has to decide whether she can allow anyone to love her again. Beloved evokes both the peril of motherhood and its singular power. Reading it, I wanted to fold myself into the pages and then fall out of my skin. It’s painful, but what’s even more devastating is that the novel is one of the most banned books in America. When I clicked on the message, I was relieved and then annoyed by the next words: “—Jon Ossoff,” under an image of the senator from Georgia staring into the middle distance, handsomely. “Last night I took the stage to debate my MAGA extremist opponent Mike Collins,” “Ossoff” went on to tell me.
